answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB accounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name my-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 failoverPriority=0 --default-consistency-level Session. (This is part of the core az CLI, not an extra extension for basic account management.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (set kind or apiProperties to MongoDB). Example Bicep resource: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'my-account' kind: 'MongoDB' properties: { ... } }. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account; for MongoDB DB/collection use azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) connection string example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@my-account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. SRV variant: mongodb+srv://myUser@my-account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port commonly used for TLS is 10255. ssl=true (TLS) and replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false are normally required.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos (DocumentDB) billed by provisioned throughput (RUs/sec) or serverless/autoscale RUs. There is also a newer vCore/dedicated cluster offering for MongoDB-compatible workloads (dedicated compute tiers billed by vCores/M-series sizes) in some SKUs. In practice expect RU-based billing for classic Cosmos accounts and a vCore-style billing for dedicated MongoDB-compatible clusters; serverless and autoscale options may also be available depending on the account type.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: MongoDB drivers connect using SCRAM-style username/password credentials backed by the Cosmos account keys or database users (i.e., standard MongoDB auth). Cosmos DB also supports resource tokens and master keys for management. Direct Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication for the MongoDB API is not generally available — unlike the Core SQL API which has Azure AD RBAC — so drivers normally use the MongoDB username/password derived from the Cosmos account or database user. (If you need Azure AD for control-plane operations, use az/REST and Azure AD; data-plane MongoDB drivers use SCRAM credentials.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is not a separate Cosmos-specific MongoDB client — do not use @azure/cosmos for MongoDB API workloads; use the MongoDB driver/mongoose.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style vector indexes use the knnVector index type (MongoDB 7+ style). Example createIndex command: db.atm_status.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knnVector: { dimension: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', indexType: 'hnsw' } }); — replace indexType with 'hnsw' or 'ivf' depending on support (DiskANN, HNSW and IVF are the index families you may see).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For basic full-text search use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})). For advanced or hybrid (text + vector) search in Azure, you typically integrate Cosmos DB/MongoDB API with Azure Cognitive Search (index Cosmos documents into Cognitive Search) or use the provider's native vector+text search if the account exposes MongoDB 7+ vector indexes combined with text indexes. There is no Atlas Search — use Azure Cognitive Search for advanced full-text/hybrid scenarios if native support is missing.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports specific MongoDB wire protocol versions depending on the account configuration (commonly up through recent versions such as 3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and in newer accounts 6.0/7.0 if configured). Not all server-side/admin commands are supported; some admin commands, server-side JavaScript, certain change-of-shard or cluster-admin operations, and some extensions (e.g. certain aggregation stages or commands that require server internals) may be missing or behave differently. Expect differences in transaction and aggregation semantics compared to a stock MongoDB server.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Run the official MongoDB server locally for MongoDB-API development. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name mongo-dev -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=root -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=pass mongo:7.0. (The Azure Cosmos DB emulator exists for some APIs but historically did not fully emulate the MongoDB API — for reliable local MongoDB behavior use the official mongo image on port 27017.)

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are available when the account exposes a MongoDB server version/wire protocol that supports them (MongoDB 3.6+). Typically no extra account flag is needed for standard Cosmos MongoDB clusters that advertise change-stream support, but older or restricted accounts may not support them. In application code use collection.watch(...) with fullDocument:'updateLookup' and handle resume tokens; if change streams are not available you'll get an error from the driver.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Assuming the corporate MCP naming, the service-specific MCP server would be 'documentdb' (or the documentdb MCP profile). The general Azure MCP server covers control-plane operations, but for document/Mongo-specific data-plane inspection you should use the 'documentdb' MCP server tooling/profile that points at the MongoDB-compatible endpoint.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for Microsoft's JSON document database service; it was rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API' is an API surface that exposes MongoDB wire protocol compatibility on top of the Cosmos engine. This is distinct from any independently named open-source 'DocumentDB' project — Cosmos is Microsoft's managed engine implementing multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the hood it's the Cosmos DB engine implementing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol (not a stock mongod process). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect differences in supported commands, consistency/transaction semantics, and performance characteristics. Some admin/server-level features present in upstream MongoDB may be missing or behave differently.

answers.question: Which database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_banking_16 for all collections and operations.

answers.question: What vector index definition does this sample rely on for ATM embedding search?
answers.answer: Create a knnVector index on the embedding field. Example: db.atm_status.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knnVector: { dimension: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', indexType: 'hnsw' } });

answers.question: What collection names and basic schemas will the sample create?
answers.answer: Collections: 1) atm_status — documents { _id, atmId, timestamp, status: 'online'|'offline'|'low_cash', cashLevel:number, embedding: [float], metadata: {...} }. 2) network_summary — single document { _id:'network_summary', totalATMs, onlineCount, offlineCount, lowCashCount, lastUpdated }. 3) alerts — documents { _id, atmId, alertType, severity, timestamp, resolved:false }.

answers.question: How will the sample open and use change streams to detect status changes?
answers.answer: Use the MongoDB driver's watch API: const stream = collection.watch([{ $match: { 'updateDescription.updatedFields.status': { $exists: true } } }], { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); Use resume tokens and fullDocument:'updateLookup' to get the current doc on updates and handle interruptions by saving the last resume token to resume the stream.

answers.question: How should the app read the cluster connection string and what mongoose options to use?
answers.answer: Read connection string from env DOCUMENTDB_URI (do not hardcode). Connect example: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false, authSource: 'admin' }); (Adjust options to match the cluster's required params.)
